summary:
We developed MarsWalk Atlas, an integrated mapping and mission-planning system designed to help future astronauts safely explore the surface of Mars. Our project combines data from multiple NASA Mars missions into one interactive map with six important layers: terrain, minerals, ground strength, weather, radiation, and subsurface conditions.
The main challenge is the difficulty of navigating Mars safely due to its harsh environment, unpredictable weather, radiation exposure, and uneven terrain. We address this by combining these datasets into a unified 1-metre grid and calculating a Walk Score based on safety, speed, and scientific value. Our system also recommends suitable walking routes, identifies potential hazards, and provides live Go/No-Go safety checks.
This project is important because it can support safer human exploration, reduce mission risks, save time and resources, and help astronauts identify scientifically valuable locations. Our ultimate goal is to make future human Marswalks safer, smarter, and more productive.
details:
MarsWalk Atlas is a layered map for planning and carrying out a Marswalk. It fuses six NASA data layers: terrain (MGS MOLA, MRO HiRISE/CTX), minerals (CRISM, PIXL), ground strength (THEMIS), weather (MEDA), radiation (MAVEN, RAD) and subsurface (SHARAD, RIMFAX, InSight). Each 1 m cell gets a Walk Score (Safety × Speed × Science), refreshed every sol. Astronauts plan routes, follow a suit heads-up display, then feed new findings back into the map. Live Go/No-Go gates track dust, radiation, temperature, comms and life-support margins. We demonstrate it on a sample route in Jezero Crater.

Benefits and impact: safer, faster decisions and more science per walk, with one view replacing six datasets. It could also support robotic traverses and Moon missions.

Tools: Node.js (pptxgenjs), Python (NumPy, Pillow), react-icons, sharp and LibreOffice for the deck. The full Atlas would use open NASA data with GIS tools such as GDAL and QGIS.

Creativity: a single decision score, time-aware mapping and science-weighted routing.

Factors considered: crew safety first, differing data resolutions, comms delay, glanceable displays, and honesty that the route and thresholds are illustrative.
